pricing.freeTierCaps: 30 attendee credits per year; 30-minute sessions; 10 events per organization; 20 sessions per event; 10 automated actions per event
pricing.billingTerms: annual only under the current attendee-credit model; auto-renews yearly
pricing.hiddenCosts: One credit is consumed whenever one external attendee joins one session, including replay/on-demand viewing; the same person consumes another credit in a different session. New attendees are blocked when credits run out unless an Enterprise contract permits overage. AI Studio, live translation, extra workspaces, regional hosting, SSO, restreaming, RTMP input and extra API calls are add-ons.

verdictSummary: A consolation build is possible, but the paid product's decisive value sits outside a solo rebuild. For Livestorm, run a small browser webinar with registrations and a simple replay page. The hard boundary is global media, email delivery, engagement, integrations, analytics, and reliability, plus real-time media infrastructure and reliability.
coreLoopDIY: Run a small browser webinar with registrations, issue signed room links, publish a simple replay page, and keep recordings only when every participant is clearly informed.
whatYouLose: global media, email delivery, engagement, integrations, analytics, and reliability
ongoingBurden: TURN capacity, codecs, browsers, packet loss, scaling, recording, consent, abuse, monitoring, and incident response
whyPeopleStillPay: People still pay for Livestorm because video products survive because real-time media quality and global reliability are infrastructure businesses, not weekend interface projects. The recurring cost buys TURN capacity, codecs, browsers, packet loss, scaling, recording, consent, abuse, monitoring, and incident response, not just the visible interface.

rejectedAlternatives.name: BigBlueButton
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Good live room, wrong product: registration pages and replay marketing are still your job.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Jitsi Meet
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A meeting room is not a webinar platform; registrations, reminders and replay pages are absent.

notes: Editorial comparison targets the Pro plan and a small private meeting service DIY substitute. Recheck price before merge.
prompt:
Build a closest honest personal substitute for Livestorm in an empty repository.
Use Docker Compose, Jitsi Meet, a small Next.js 15 control panel, PostgreSQL, and TURN; do not offer alternative stacks.
The core loop is: run a small browser webinar with registrations, issue signed room links, publish a simple replay page, and keep recordings only when every participant is clearly informed.
Make the first run work locally with one documented command.
Store all user data locally by default and make export straightforward.
Put secrets in .env, ship .env.example, and never commit credentials.
Deploy Jitsi Meet through pinned Docker images and configure a dedicated TURN service.
Build an owner panel for rooms, signed invitations, expiry, lobby mode, and participant limits.
Show connection diagnostics for camera, microphone, browser, bandwidth, and TURN reachability.
Make recording disabled by default and require an on-screen consent state for every participant.
Store room metadata and audit events, but do not store media unless explicitly enabled.
Add health checks, bandwidth dashboards, backup, restore, upgrade, and incident instructions.
Include clear empty, loading, success, and recoverable error states.
Add input validation, safe filenames, and graceful handling of unavailable APIs.
Write focused tests for the core transformation and one end-to-end happy path.
Create a README with setup, architecture, permissions, data location, and backup steps.
Do not add accounts, billing, telemetry, analytics, or a hosted control plane.
Do not claim to reproduce proprietary data, network liquidity, regulated access, or frontier infrastructure.
Deliberately leave out a global media edge network.
Deliberately leave out public webinar scale and telephony.
Deliberately leave out regulated recording, enterprise compliance, and guaranteed support.
Finish by running the tests and listing the exact commands used.
